title: Extreme heat is already reducing firm sales, productivity, and wages in MENAAP while climate trade rules and adaptation finance reshape competitiveness
source_unit: World Bank, Competing in the Face of Climate Risks: Evidence from Firms and Policy Priorities in MENAAP, 2026
geography: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan firms, workers, sectors, trade links, and policy systems

observations.period: 2026 report; firm exposure to extreme heat

denominator.unit: firms in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan covered by World Bank climate-risk analysis

firms_extreme_heat.unit: percent of firms operating in extreme heat conditions for more than 100 days per year

heat_endpoint.value: rising temperatures are already affecting sales, productivity, wages, and operating conditions

regional_exposure.value: MENAAP countries are among the most water-scarce and increasingly exposed to climate risks

observations.method: World Bank cross-country firm-level evidence and policy analysis linking temperature exposure, firm performance, labor outcomes, and climate-responsive reforms.
observations.uncertainty: The regional estimate summarizes firm exposure and does not imply identical heat conditions, adaptation, or losses across countries, sectors, firm sizes, or workers.
observations.subgroup: Firms, workers, smaller businesses, financially constrained firms, sectors with different heat sensitivity, and communities dependent on exposed firms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Firms can adapt through cooling, work redesign, water management, technology, relocation, and investment; exposure is not equivalent to irreversible loss.

observations.period: 2026; estimated marginal effect of additional hot days

denominator.unit: firm-level temperature-performance relationship estimated in the World Bank report

labor_productivity_change.unit: percent associated change in labor productivity

observations.method: World Bank firm-level empirical analysis of temperature changes and outcomes, with sector and country comparisons and adaptation-policy interpretation.
observations.uncertainty: These are reported estimated associations from the study’s specification, not universal causal constants; adaptation, baseline climate, sector mix, measurement, and omitted factors can change the relationship.
observations.subgroup: Firms and workers in heat-exposed sectors, with particular attention to smaller and more financially constrained firms facing larger losses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed losses can be reduced by adaptation investment, financing, management changes, cooling, water efficiency, and occupational protections; some firms or sectors may benefit from climate shifts.

denominator.unit: MENAAP firms and sectors exposed to destination-market climate mitigation policies

trade_policy_route.value: EU and UK carbon-border adjustment policies can affect exports, investment patterns, and sector competitiveness

carbon_intensive_sectors.value: carbon-intensive sectors face particular exposure to changing destination-market requirements

firm_response.value: green competitiveness, emissions measurement, energy efficiency, and access to adaptation finance become competitive capabilities

observations.method: World Bank analysis of MENAAP firm exposure to climate-related trade measures, including EU and UK CBAM channels, foreign investment, and sector competitiveness.
observations.uncertainty: Trade-policy effects depend on implementation, exemptions, embedded-emissions measurement, exchange rates, firm adaptation, and destination-market demand; the report does not imply uniform export losses.
observations.subgroup: Exporters, carbon-intensive industries, small and large firms, foreign investors, trade authorities, workers, and destination-market buyers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate standards can create incentives for cleaner production, new investment, and market access if firms receive finance, measurement capacity, technology, and predictable rules.

denominator.unit: MENAAP private-sector adaptation and climate-opportunity policy frame

cooling_opportunity.unit: billion US dollars projected size of a sustainable cooling industry opportunity

double_dividend.value: climate-responsive reforms can help firms adapt while addressing productivity, investment, and competitiveness barriers

priority_reforms.value: improve access to finance, ease business-environment bottlenecks, support green competitiveness, and strengthen private-sector adaptation

observations.method: World Bank policy analysis of adaptation, cooling, investment, finance, productivity, business conditions, and green-sector opportunity in MENAAP.
observations.uncertainty: The cooling figure is a projection, not realized investment or employment; reform benefits depend on finance, regulation, technology, energy access, and distribution of gains.
observations.subgroup: Cooling firms, energy providers, investors, smaller businesses, workers, households, regulators, and communities exposed to extreme heat.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cooling can reduce heat stress and protect productivity but may increase energy demand or affordability pressure unless efficient, low-carbon, and accessible technologies are deployed.

related_sources.claim: World Bank official release summarizes reported firm-level heat effects and the cooling opportunity.
Official reproducibility package for the report’s firm, climate, adaptation, and trade analyses.
Official reproducibility-package DOI and report evidence resource.

boundary: This record adds a firm-climate-to-worker and trade-competitiveness route linking heat exposure, sales, productivity, wages, adaptation finance, carbon-border measures, and cooling opportunities. It is not a household heat-stress estimate, a universal causal effect, a firm census, or respondent-level microdata analysis.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank report page, press release, and reproducibility catalog were reviewed; heat exposure, estimated firm effects, smaller-firm vulnerability, climate-trade channels, adaptation reforms, and cooling opportunity claims were cross-checked.
